headline: The Forecast for Christmas Is Muddy

paragraphs.text: Snowville, New Hampshire, was named for Joseph Snow, who moved there after fighting in the War of 1812, but the village gets more than its fair share of wintry precipitation. Over the past 10 years, nine of its Christmases have been white.

This year, the chance of a white Christmas—an inch or more of snow on the ground on Christmas morning—is currently about 65 percent in Snowville, according to an online tool from the Weather Company. That’s not too shabby, but it’s also a drop of about 15 percent from normal. The culprit is probably this year’s super El Niño, which is poised to scramble winter weather across the country.

During El Niño, which is part of a climatological cycle that’s been around for at least 250 million years, the winds that normally push west across the Pacific weaken. Warm water starts to pile up around South America. As heat moves from the water into the atmosphere above it, weather patterns change. In the United States, El Niño generally results in a hotter North and a soggier, cooler South.

By itself, El Niño doesn’t warm the planet; it moves existing heat around. But these days, there is more heat than ever to rearrange. “When you throw an El Niño on the shoulders of climate change, we expect that a lot of the country is going to experience above-average temperatures,” Shel Winkley, the chief meteorologist at the nonpartisan science-communication group Climate Central, told me. The odds, he said, lean toward less snow across the U.S., especially in areas where a white Christmas is the norm.

Instead, brace for the possibility of mud. In many places around the country, “brown Christmas is possible,” Shuyi Chen, a meteorology professor at the University of Washington, told me. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s latest Winter Outlook report indicates a roughly 80 percent chance that forceful El Niño conditions will continue through the new year, bringing extra rain to the southern part of the country, especially the Southeast. Florida has already experienced serious flooding in recent weeks; so, too, have California and the Four Corners region.

Brown Christmas is not guaranteed, though. Seven Christmases have coincided with an El Niño since 2003, and snow cover has varied dramatically among them. In 2009, a blizzard blanketed more than half of the mainland United States. In 2023, less than a fifth of the Lower 48 collected snow cover. Plus, this El Niño is coinciding with record-high ocean temperatures and is predicted to be the most powerful since 1950, which means that scientists lack a perfect historical parallel from which to make predictions about this season’s snowfall. Besides, weather is inherently fickle. Forecasters won’t be able to predict how day-to-day fluctuations may interact with the effects of El Niño on Christmas until a week or two in advance.

Perhaps the biggest wild card for the December forecast is the polar vortex, Daniel Cayan, a climate scientist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, told me. This band of strong winds locks in extremely cold air at the top of the globe. The winds arise each fall, when the farthest reaches of the Northern Hemisphere start receiving little sunlight, causing air-temperature differences between the Arctic and the equator to grow. When the sunlight returns in spring, it heats the Arctic stratosphere and causes the vortex to crumble. The dissolving polar vortex can bring about periods of intense cold in the continental U.S. as far south as Florida, and with them, an increased chance of snow.

Usually, the polar vortex deteriorates in March or April; this year, it’s already starting to break down. Researchers aren’t yet sure why, but they have theories. Climate change may play a role. The Arctic is warming nearly four times faster than the rest of the world, and sea ice is growing sparser, which may allow heat to move more easily from the polar ocean to the atmosphere. A warmer Arctic narrows that crucial temperature difference with lower latitudes, weakening the polar vortex and allowing more frigid air to escape to the south.

Whether many Americans will have a muddy Christmas or a white one comes down in large part to a tug-of-war between two age-old phenomena, each of which is behaving abnormally this year. Experts can’t predict exactly how the interaction will play out. Ben Kirtman, an atmospheric-sciences professor at the University of Miami, told me that if sudden warming in the Arctic enables cold air to break out of the polar vortex, it could mean snow.

But without such a well-timed gust, the persistent force of El Niño seems likelier to win out. This year’s super El Niño has already been associated with severe coastal erosion in California, a parade of major hurricanes in the Pacific, and sea turtles showing up far from their normal habitat. A wobbly polar vortex may be no match for it.
